To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
perceived performance and perceived disconfirmation are the largest contributors to citizen satisfaction, and no significant impact on satisfaction is identified from civil infrastructure projects.

the expectancy disconfirmation theory can be used to assess the impact of HCA projects on HN citizen satisfaction with government services, and that the expectancy disconfirm theory can be applied to HN government services to assess the impact on citizen satisfaction.
the expectancy disconfirmation theory of citizen satisfaction is applicable in a developing nation, and that the impact of civil investment on citizen satisfaction is negligible.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of HCA projects on the HN citizens.
the impact of U.S. investments for infrastructure development in foreign countries.

the impact of civil engineering infrastructure on citizen satisfaction of HN government services and how this can be applied in future DoD exercises to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of U.S. assistance in foreign nations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
civil infrastructure projects are not an effective method of improving HN citizen satisfaction with government services.
civil infrastructure projects do not significantly impact citizen satisfaction with government services in developing countries.

the investment of civil infrastructures in foreign countries has no impact on HN citizen satisfaction, however, perceived performance and disconfirmations have the greatest impact on citizen satisfaction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the U.S. government should consider citizen satisfaction when selecting HCA projects.

the U.S. government should consider the citizen's perspective of HN government services prior to investing in HCA projects and that the U.S., HN, and international organizations should work together to develop and utilize a standardized method of measuring the impact of HCA projects on HN citizen satisfaction.
the U.S. government can use the proposed precursors to select civil infrastructure projects for HCA activities that are more likely to improve citizen satisfaction of government service delivery.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the U.S. should invest in civil infrastructure in developing countries that will improve the lives of citizens, but the U.S. must also be aware of the limitations of civil infrastructure projects to improve citizen satisfaction with government services.
the U.S. government should not use the construction of civil infrastructure projects as the primary tool to improve citizen satisfaction.
we have identified that perceived performance and the disconfirmation of expectations are the largest factors that influence citizen satisfaction.
